commentary.meaning: One number, said three times. The verse gives her sixty-four acts of ritual attendance, then declares her to be made of the sixty-four arts, then surrounds her with yoginīs reckoned in sixty-four crores. The three names move outward in a way that is easy to miss: the first is what a worshipper does to her, the second is what she consists of, the third is who else is in the room. Between them they take a number that in Indian culture simply means a complete set and use it to describe a rite, a curriculum and a retinue. The middle name is the interesting one. To say that she is made of the sixty-four arts is to say that singing, painting, carpentry, cookery, gem-testing and the training of parrots are not activities performed in her presence but material she is composed of, which is a considerably stronger claim about the world than the surrounding verses have been making.
commentary.history:
Sixty-four is four cubed, and it recurs across Indian learning wherever a set needs to be marked as complete: sixty-four tantras, sixty-four yoginīs, sixty-four bhairavas, sixty-four arts, and here sixty-four ritual services. It is not a count arrived at by counting. It is a shape the mind can hold, in the same way that a hundred and eight is, and lists that carry the number regularly turn out to contain a different number of items when you actually enumerate them.

The upacāras are the most concrete thing in the verse, and the least often explained. Upacāra means an approach or an attendance — literally a going-near — and the underlying idea is domestic hospitality: what you do for an honoured guest who has come to your house. Ordinary image-worship uses sixteen of them, the ṣoḍaśopacāra, and most temple ritual anywhere in India is a variant of that list. The elaborate Śrīvidyā rite uses sixty-four, and they are worth reading in order at least once, because they are not sixty-four kinds of incense. They are a morning. The old ornaments are taken off; there is a massage with scented oil; she is led into the bathing hall and seated on a jewelled stool; hot water; drying; red silk and a red upper cloth; then into the anointing hall for sandal, aloe, saffron, musk, camphor; incense held under the mass of her hair; garlands of jasmine, campaka, aśoka; then into the jewel hall for the crown of nine gems, the crescent, vermilion in the parting of the hair, collyrium, earrings, a nose ornament, lac for the lower lip; then necklaces, armlets by the pair, bangles, rings, girdle, anklets; then the noose in one hand, the goad in another, the sugarcane bow in the third, the flower arrows in the fourth; then she mounts the great cakra and takes her seat on Kāmeśvara's lap; then a cup of nectar, water for the mouth, camphored betel, laughter; then the waving of lamps, the parasol, two fly-whisks, a mirror, a fan. The list ends with scent, flower, incense, lamp and food — which is to say that the sixty-four services finish at the point where an ordinary short worship begins.

Kalā in the second name is one of the great multipurpose words of Sanskrit and this is the verse to learn it in. Its root sense is a small division of something larger. From that it means a sixteenth part; a digit of the moon; a fraction of time; and, in the sense used here, a skill or an art, a discrete competence that can be enumerated and taught. All the meanings stay alive at once, so catuḥṣaṣṭikalāmayī can be heard as made of the sixty-four arts and equally as made of sixty-four parts. The word will matter again: this recension divides the thousand names into kalās, and the moon and the sun are each said to have their own set of them.

The standard list of the sixty-four arts is Vātsyāyana's, in the third chapter of the first book of the Kāmasūtra, where they are prescribed as the education of a cultivated person alongside the Kāmasūtra itself. Other lists exist and differ; his is simply the best known. What is striking about it is how unhierarchical it is. Singing, instrumental music, dance and painting come first, but the same list contains the cutting of stencils for face-decoration, arrangements of coloured rice and flowers, the making of flower-beds, tooth powders and body paints, water-games, garland design, perfumery, conjuring, sleight of hand, cookery, the mixing of drinks, needlework, riddles, recitation, carpentry, architecture, the testing of gems, metallurgy, arboriculture, the arranging of cock and quail fights, teaching parrots and mynas to talk, massage, codes and secret writing, knowledge of regional languages, prosody, lexicography, and physical training. A goddess who is made of that list is being credited with skill as such, from the highest art to the most domestic knack.

The last name is the loudest and the least literal. A koṭi is ten million, so sixty-four koṭis is six hundred and forty million yoginīs, and no one is being asked to audit the figure. But the sixty-four yoginīs behind the hyperbole were the object of a real and geographically specific cult, and it left buildings. Circular open-air temples survive at Hirapur and Ranipur-Jharial in Odisha, at Bheraghat near Jabalpur, and at Mitaoli in the Morena district, most of them built between the ninth and the twelfth centuries. They are round, roofless, and lined on the inside with niches, each niche holding one goddess facing the centre. The lists of names differ from site to site, and the number is sometimes eighty-one instead of sixty-four. When this verse says she is served by troops of yoginīs it is not inventing a decorative crowd; it is invoking a form of worship that people once walked into.
commentary.practice:
This verse is the hardest thing to say in the whole of this stretch of the stotra, and the difficulty is concentrated in one word. Catuḥṣaṣṭi is catur, four, plus ṣaṣṭi, sixty — Sanskrit counts four-and-sixty, like the older English. The r of catur has become a visarga before the sibilant, and ṣaṣṭi itself has a retroflex sibilant followed by a retroflex stop. So in five syllables you have a visarga, then ṣ, then ṣṭ. The tongue-tip curls back and stays back. Say ca-tuḥ-ṣaṣ-ṭi at half speed until the two ṣ sounds are identical to each other and neither of them has drifted forward into an English "sh".

Then the compound makes it worse. In catuḥṣaṣṭyupacārāḍhyā, the final i of ṣaṣṭi meets the u of upacāra and becomes the glide y, which is the sandhi rule that turns i into y before any dissimilar vowel. That leaves the cluster ṣṭy: retroflex sibilant, retroflex stop, palatal glide, three articulations with the tongue moving back, staying back, then springing forward. And the word ends in āḍhyā, which is an aspirated retroflex ḍh followed by y. Two of the nastiest clusters in the language are in one word, and there is no way round them except slowly.

Against that, the second half of the first line is a rest. Catuḥṣaṣṭikalāmayī has no conjunct after the opening, and the suffix -mayī, feminine of -maya, means simply made of — the same suffix as in cinmayī three verses later. Let the line relax there.

The second line is one name of sixteen syllables: mahācatuḥṣaṣṭikoṭiyoginīgaṇasevitā. The caesura falls after the eighth syllable, which lands inside the word between koṭi and yoginī. Hear the pause without opening a gap in the sound, the same discipline the fourth meditation verse asks for. Yoginī has a plain dental n and gaṇa has a retroflex ṇ, and they are three syllables apart, so this is another of the free drills the stotra keeps handing out.

One small grammatical point that helps the sense. Āḍhya means rich in, well supplied with, and it governs an instrumental: rich by means of the sixty-four services. Mayī means consisting of. Sevitā is a past passive participle, waited upon. So the three names are grammatically three different relations — she is enriched by the first sixty-four, composed of the second, attended by the third — and knowing that keeps the verse from sounding like a chant on a single number.

In archanā the names become catuḥṣaṣṭyupacārāḍhyāyai namaḥ and so on, which is a mouthful worth attempting precisely because it forces the ṣṭy cluster to be produced twice in one breath. If you can manage that dative you have solved the verse.

What to hold while chanting: the number is a claim about scope, not about quantity. Sixty-four means all of them.

crossReferences.translation: Singing. Instrumental music. Dancing. Painting. The cutting of stencils for facial decoration. … These sixty-four are the subordinate branches of learning, of which the Kāmasūtra is the whole.
crossReferences.relevance: The list the second name is counting. Only the first five items are given here; the remaining fifty-nine run from flower arrangement and perfumery through carpentry, gem-testing and metallurgy to codes, dictionaries and physical training. Note the fifth item, viśeṣakacchedya: viśeṣaka is the forehead mark that this stotra applied in its fifth verse, and here it is a skill with its own technique and its own stencils.

crossReferences.translation: Let him perform the sixty-four services. Every service-mantra is to be made with the three seed-syllables at the front and the words "I set this in place; homage" at the end. Taking off the ornaments; a massage with scented oil; entering the bathing hall; … a bath in hot water; … putting on the red silk; … a crown of nine gems, the crescent of the moon, vermilion for the parting of the hair; … scent, flower, incense, lamp, food — I set these in place; homage. Having thus performed the sixty-four services …
crossReferences.relevance: The first name of this verse, described from the inside. Only a handful of the sixty-four are quoted here; in the manual they run continuously from undressing to the last mouthful. Two things are worth noticing. Each item is grammatically an accusative governed by kalpayāmi, "I furnish, I set in place", so the whole rite is a single sentence. And the sequence ends with the five offerings that ordinary worship consists of, so the elaborate rite is not a substitute for the simple one but a very long approach to it.

references.title: Yoginī Cult and Temples: A Tantric Tradition
references.author: Vidya Dehejia (National Museum, New Delhi, 1986)
references.note: The standard survey of the circular sixty-four yoginī temples, with plans, photographs and the surviving name-lists set side by side. The best answer to the question of what the third name of this verse is actually referring to, and a reminder that these goddesses had architecture before they had a place in a hymn.

references.note: For the sixty-four arts in the first book, and for the reminder that they were a syllabus rather than an allegory. The translators' notes explain several items that make no sense from the bare list — what exactly is being cut in viśeṣakacchedya, and why teaching a parrot to speak counted as an accomplishment.
